newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan firm reaps profits from receding hairlines.
newsitem.headline: Japan firm reaps profits from receding hairlines.

text.p: Baldness is a growth industry in Japan, where more and more men are losing their hair due to the stresses and strains of urban life.
The daily grind of long commutes, career pressure and a switch from healthy fare like sushi to a more Western-style diet are taking an increasing toll on Japanese locks.
But one person's hair loss is another's financial gain.
Wig makers like industry leaders Aderans Co Ltd and unlisted Art Nature Inc are reaping the benefits of the balding pates, and analysts say business should keep booming.
Some of their best customers are younger men who are keen to keep baldness at bay using special treatments or discreet toupees designed to augment their own thinning hair.

"Young men in their 20s especially are extremely sensitive about hair," said a spokeswoman at Aderans. "We help them hang on to their tresses and make the switch to hairpieces that are so discreet even their girlfriends don't notice."

Aderans, which has 40 percent of the 80 billion yen ($634 million) market, started selling custom-made wigs a quarter of a century ago, repairing the wounded pride of balding men across Japan. But four years ago, the firm launched special treatments for controlling hair loss with massages, counselling and pore-cleansing, which last for an hour and cost anything from 10,000 yen ($79) to 15,000 yen ($119).

Aderans's parent current profit surged by nearly 148 percent the year the new treatments were launched. ING Barings Securities Japan Ltd sees Aderans's parent current profit -- which includes investment income -- leaping 34 percent in the year to February 28, 1997, to 8.98 billion yen ($71.2 million).

"The only major rival is unlisted Art Nature Inc and newcomers would have to invest heavily in a convincing advertising scheme to cultivate customers," said Robert Burghart, ING Barings senior analyst.

Aderans customers can have human or artificial hair woven in with their own tresses. Wigs and toupees ranging from 70,000 yen ($555) to 720,000 yen ($5,714), depending on the size and number of hairs implanted, can be made to order.

"The strength of the firm lies in the fact that it takes customers from the initial stages of baldness to actually donning a wig," said Shinji Tomita, analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics. "Long-term customers translate into long-term profits."
Scientists have attributed the growing baldness problem to a range of factors including stress and a changing diet.

But Japanese men, of whom an estimated 21.08 percent are balding, are still more hirsute than their U.S. counterparts. In the United States, some 34.19 percent of the male population suffers hair loss, according to wig industry data.
Nevertheless, interest is keener in Japan, says Aderans, which also has operations overseas.

"Japanese have black hair and when it gets sparse, it is noticeable, but Caucasians have lighter coloured hair and the losses are not as obvious," the spokeswoman said. Japanese also prefer toupees to ready-made wigs covering the complete pate, which are preferred abroad, she said.
"A blond Caucasian can become a redhead without looking odd," she said. "Japanese prefer to improve their looks by subtly enhancing the areas that need it most."

Analysts predict stable growth in the years ahead, citing the industry's relative immunity to external factors such as tax hikes and the health of the economy. Japan's sales tax was raised from three percent to five percent this month.

"Men are ready, any day, to pay an extra two percent to look good," Burghart said. "Unless being bald becomes the dominating trend, it is highly unlikely that the profitability of the company (Aderans) will be harmed." ($1=126 yen)
